keywords.term: intraoperative facial cortico-bulbar motor evoked potentials monitoring

div.head: | Introduction
div.p: Vestibular schwannomas, also called acoustic neuromas, are fibrous tumors that arise from Schwann cells of the vestibulocochlear nerve and make up > 75% of all cerebellopontine angle (CPA) tumors. Meningiomas account for another 10%-15% of CPA tumors, with atypical meningioma representing a minor subset of this pathology. Patients with CPA tumors typically present with progressive sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and vestibular symptoms from cranial nerve (CN) VIII compression. In some cases, trigeminal distribution numbness or pain may result from compression of CN V, or very rarely, facial weakness from CN VII involvement may occur [1].

We present a case of sudden onset unilateral complete flaccid facial paralysis on the day of planned resection of ipsilateral CPA angle tumor. She experienced complete recovery of facial paralysis immediately after translabyrinthine approach to tumor and internal auditory canal (IAC) decompression. Return of facial function was predicted by intraoperative facial cortico-bulbar motor evoked potentials (MEPs).

div.head: | Case Report
div.p: A 49-year-old healthy female initially presented with right sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance, with no facial weakness. Her contrast-enhanced MRI Brain 3 months later revealed a 2.6 × 2.0 × 1.5 cm lesion in the right CPA that extended into the right IAC (Figure 1A,B). By the time of her pre-op appointment 4 months later, she had elected for a translabyrinthine approach for microsurgical resection of a suspected vestibular schwannoma. She continued to have normal and symmetric facial movement (HB I/VI). She had unilateral right ear profound moderately severe sensorineural hearing loss of 250-4000 Hz, sloping back to profound hearing loss of 6-8000 Hz, with no response at equipment limits at 8000 Hz (Figure 2). While pulling into the parking lot on the morning of surgery, she suffered a sudden onset of complete flaccid right-sided facial paralysis and decreased sensation (V1-V3). CT head w/o contrast (Figure 1C,D) showed a stable mass with no evidence of intratumoral hemorrhage or other acute changes. After discussion and with her informed consent, she underwent translabyrinthine exposure craniotomy for bony decompression of the tumor in the posterior fossa and IAC, with a plan for a staged return to the OR for tumor resection after a period of facial nerve recovery.

To monitor the integrity of the facial nerve intraoperatively, conventional electromyography (EMG) and transcranial facial cortico-bulbar MEP monitoring were performed. Paired subdermal needles (Rhythmlink, Columbia, SC, USA) were placed on the scalp using a modified protocol as described by Toczylowski et al. [2] The anode was placed either at C3-CP3 or C4-CP4 and the cathode was placed either at C1-CP1 or C2-CP2 to transcranially stimulate the facial motor area contralateral to the tumor side. Recording electrodes were placed on the orbicularis oculi (OOc), orbicularis oris (OOr) and mentalis muscle ipsilateral to the tumor side. A short train of 6-8 pulses of 0.075 ms duration with interstimulus interval (ISI) of 1-2 ms, followed by a single pulse 100 ms later, was applied to obtain reproducible central responses. Stimulation intensity and intensity up to 150-250 V was applied. Intraoperative facial MEP prior to decompression demonstrated limited or completely absent facial nerve function at OOc, OOr, and mentalis (Figure 3A). Standard conventional EMG monitoring during the translabyrinthine approach did not result in activation during drilling in the descending and labyrinthine segments of the facial nerve, and the nerve remained bony covered throughout its course. Given the possibility of facial schwannoma and the potential unreliability of EMG monitoring in the setting of paralysis, sampling for frozen specimen analysis and tumor debulking were deferred. Immediately post-decompression of the widened and tumor-filled internal auditory canal via translabyrinthine craniotomy (Figure 4A), facial MEPs demonstrated recovered evoked potentials of the OOr and mentalis (Figure 3B). Immediately post-surgery, she had complete recovery of facial symmetry (HB I/VI bilateral face). Given the rapid return to normal facial function, it was thought that the facial palsy may have been secondary to tumor compression, and she returned to the OR 3 days later for complete tumor resection with facial nerve preservation (Figure 4B). At the beginning of tumor dissection, facial MEPs revealed robust facial nerve function in OOc, OOr, and mentalis, which were maintained post-resection (Figure 3C). Conventional EMG recording returned negative stimulation responses over the entire posterior surface of the tumor prior to debulking and also later revealed the nerve to be electrically intact throughout the time of facial nerve dissection as it took an anterior-superior course in relation to the tumor. Her recovery from these surgeries was uncomplicated. Her post-op facial sensation and motor function remained normal (Figure 5) with returned sensation of V1-V3 at 1 week follow-up. Somewhat surprisingly, pathology returned as atypical meningioma, WHO grade II, for which ongoing surveillance with imaging is planned. At last follow-up, she reported improvement in all preoperative symptoms aside from hearing.

div.head: | Discussion
div.p: This case is unique in that (1) sudden onset facial paralysis in the setting of a known CPA angle tumor and complete recovery of facial nerve function immediately upon decompression has not been described; and (2) intraoperative facial MEP monitoring, while incompletely established in its effectiveness, predicted recovery of facial nerve function. Sudden facial paralysis associated with CPA tumors is uncommon and not completely understood. In the setting of known CPA tumors, it has been reported that 47% of vestibular schwannomas with intratumoral hemorrhage may present with facial nerve palsy [3]. In our case, facial schwannoma also remained on the differential initially. Though less likely, viral or idiopathic inflammatory insults to the nerve are still possible in the setting of a CPA tumor. Inflammatory tumor paracrine signaling contributing to worse facial nerve outcomes has also been described, though that often occurs in synchronous tumors of the CPA [4].

The challenge of preserving facial nerve function during CPA tumor resection warrants innovative nerve monitoring techniques [5]. We routinely utilize direct and triggered facial nerve stimulation and concurrent facial muscle EMG recording. However, confirmation of the electrical integrity of the facial nerve using standard facial nerve monitoring requires stimulation at its root entry zone or at a point in the cisternal segment of the nerve proximal to the tumor, which can be challenging due to tumor size, distorted anatomy, and false positive responses. Intraoperative facial MEP recordings were developed to provide real-time, quantitative, and functional assessment of the entire innervation pathway from upper motor neurons in the motor cortex, through the cortico-bulbar tract, facial nucleus, and facial nerve, and terminating in the muscles of facial expression [5]. Although our institution utilizes transcranial MEP during microvascular decompression of trigeminal nerve and facial nerve, overall limited literature and experience on this use exist in practice [4]. Herein, we observed a strong correlation with facial nerve function recovery following initial IAC decompression intraoperatively in the OOr and mentalis, with complete recovery noted by the time of resection 3 days later, including the OOc. This supports the improvements in facial motor evoked potentials reported in a patient with improved facial nerve function after microsurgical removal of a vestibular schwannoma with repeated intratumoral hemorrhage [3]. We describe a case of sudden onset facial paralysis from atypical meningioma at the CPA angle that was resolved via bony decompression with the return of facial nerve function predicted by intraoperative facial MEP. In the appropriate clinical context, physicians facing the management dilemma of acute facial paralysis in the setting of a known CPA tumor should consider the expediency of proactive surgical management.

figure.head: FIGURE 1 |
figure.figDesc: FIGURE 1 | Pre-operative MR and CT imaging and audiogram. (A) Axial and (B) coronal contrast enhanced T1 weighted MR imaging revealing an enhancing mass of the right cerebellopontine angle that extends into the right IAC. (C) Axial and (D) coronal CT imaging revealing widened IAC and absence of significant calcification within the right cerebellopontine angle tumor.

figure.head: FIGURE 2 |
figure.figDesc: FIGURE 2 | Pre-operative audiogram and speech testing. (A) Audiogram revealing right sided profound sensorineural hearing loss with normal contralateral hearing. (B) No right sided word discrimination despite reaching the limits of testing.

figure.head: FIGURE 3 |
figure.figDesc: FIGURE 3 | Facial cortico-bulbar motor evoked potentials (facial MEPs), with representative tracings displayed for the following timepoints: (A) prior to translabyrinthine craniotomy decompression of the IAC; (B) after decompression; (C) after gross total tumor removal 3 days later. Tracings in green indicate pre-incision baselines and traces in pink indicate Facial MEP responses post decompression/resection.

figure.head: FIGURE 4 |
figure.figDesc: FIGURE 4 | Intraoperative microscopic photos. (A) View of decompressed internal auditory canal filled with tumor after translabyrinthine approach with posterior fossa dura intact prior to tumor removal. (B) View of tumor resection bed within the cerebellopontine angle after gross total tumor resection with posterior fossa having been divided and retracted. The intact cisternal segment of the facial nerve is in view. Yellow lines = widened IAC; blue line = bony covered facial nerve in its second genu and descending segment; purple circle = decompressed jugular bulb; green lines = posterior fossa dura; light purple bars = temporal lobe dura.

figure.head: FIGURE 5 |
figure.figDesc: FIGURE 5 | Post-operative photos of facial nerve function. Facial symmetry was noted (A) at rest, (B) with eye closure, and (C) with smile, with normal movement noted of all divisions including brow, mid-face, and mouth.
